newsitem.title: USA: FDA panel backs new Roche diet drug Xenical.
newsitem.headline: FDA panel backs new Roche diet drug Xenical.

text.p: A panel of Food and Drug Administration advisers on Wednesday unanimously recommended approval of new Roche Holding Ltd. diet drug Xenical.
The FDA is not bound by the panel's advice, but usually follows it.

If approved, Xenical may see U.S. sales of several hundred million dollars a year, analysts said. Xenical is not approved in any other country and has received expedited review by the FDA, according to the firm, which first applied for U.S. approval in November 1996.

The drug, which inhibits the absorption of fat, has been studied in more than 4,000 patients. According to Roche, its maximum effect is reached within a few days. Patients excrete an estimated 30 percent of fat ingested.

The panel made no specific suggestions about who should get the prescription drug, but chairman Dr. Henry Bone of the Henry Ford Hospital said that he would caution against use for longer than two years. The panel had no major safety concerns about Xenical.

The leading obesity drug, American Home Products' Redux (Dexfenfluramine), has sold well, with 3 million prescriptions written since its launch in May 1996. But it can cause a rare lung disorder in some cases and is being investigated for potential neurotoxicity.

Knoll Pharmaceuticals, a unit of BASF AG, produced an obesity drug, Meridia (Sibutramine), that was rejected by an FDA committee in September 1996 due to concerns about its tendency to slightly increase blood pressure.
Roche said Xenical helped reduce unhealthy side effects of obesity by reducing cholesterol, blood pressure and insulin levels and improving blood sugar control in diabetic patients.

Many patients experienced gastrointestinal side effects, with oily or loose stool being the primary complaint. But Roche says that these symptoms did not cause patients to drop out of trials in huge numbers.
